questions.title: Which histological findings are characteristic of Parkinson disease?
questions.question: A patient with bradykinesia, resting tremor and rigidity dies, and post-mortem examination of the brain shows loss of pigmented neurons in the substantia nigra along with intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in surviving neurons. Which protein chiefly composes these inclusions?

explanations.A: Correct. Parkinson disease is characterised histologically by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and by intracytoplasmic Lewy bodies — eosinophilic inclusions composed principally of aggregated, misfolded alpha-synuclein protein — within surviving neurons. This nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss underlies the disease's cardinal motor features, including the bradykinesia, tremor and rigidity described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Beta-amyloid is the core protein of the extracellular neuritic plaques of Alzheimer disease, not the intracytoplasmic Lewy bodies of Parkinson disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperphosphorylated tau forms the neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer disease, a different neurodegenerative disease with a different histological signature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Huntingtin is the protein whose CAG-repeat-expanded gene causes Huntington disease, characterised by caudate atrophy, not Lewy bodies.

questions.learning_objective: State that Parkinson disease is characterised histologically by Lewy bodies and loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, underlying its bradykinesia.
